documents.t: Short seasons.** By the time a traditional forecast has enough history to be confident, the selling window is half over. Size curves. AI-powered inventory optimization uses machine learning to forecast demand at the store and SKU level, detect shortage and excess inventory risk early, and recommend exactly which stock should be moved, reordered, or marked down before those problems impact sales and profitability. For multi-store retailers, it replaces spreadsheet-based inventory planning and allocation guesswork with data-driven decisions ranked by measurable business impact.

Many retail organizations still rely on a weekly planning cycle built around spreadsheets and historical reports. Sales data is collected, planners review inventory levels manually, and transfer decisions are made days after the original demand signal appeared. While this process may seem manageable, it creates two costly inventory problems.
documents.s: Why Traditional Inventory Planning Breaks in Multi-Store Retail

documents.t: A store may have strong demand for a specific item today but lack the inventory required to fulfill customer demand. For example, one location may be completely out of a popular size-38 white linen shirt while several other stores still hold excess units. The sale is lost, and often the customer is lost as well.

Excess inventory often remains trapped in locations where demand is weak. As products age, retailers eventually resort to discounts and markdowns, reducing margin that could have been protected through better allocation decisions. Both problems share the same root cause: by the time a planner notices the trend, the cheapest opportunity to act has already passed.

Traditional dashboards tell retailers what happened. AI-powered optimization platforms tell retailers what to do next. The difference is significant: **“Here is your stock cover.” versus “Move 12 units from Phuket to Bangkok today and prevent an expected stockout.” Modern AI inventory optimization platforms typically operate through four key stages.

** Cross-selling at checkout is the practice of recommending a relevant add-on at the moment a customer is already committed to buying — and it works because the hardest part of the sale is finished. The basket is open, the wallet is out, and a well-chosen suggestion feels like service, not selling.

Commitment is settled.** The customer has already decided to buy; adding one small item is a much lower barrier than the original purchase decision. Context is complete. Only at the register do you know the full basket — which makes the recommendation dramatically more relevant than any mid-aisle promotion. Attention is captive. During payment processing the customer is looking at the counter. That dwell time is either wasted or working.
documents.s: Why checkout is the best cross-sell moment in the store

documents.t: The classic approach is the cashier prompt (“would you like socks with that?”) backed by counter merchandising. Both have real limits: staff prompts are inconsistent and disappear under queue pressure, and a static counter display shows the same items to every customer regardless of what they are buying.
documents.s: Why most stores still do it badly

documents.t: React to the basket. The recommendation should fit what is being scanned — care products with leather shoes, a matching accessory with a dress — using the product and transaction context the POS already has. Keep it to one clear offer. A screen crowded with six promotions converts worse than one relevant suggestion with a strong visual. Use bundles and seasonal moments. “Complete the set” and time-boxed seasonal offers consistently outperform generic discounts. Never slow the queue. The offer must resolve in seconds — a barcode the cashier scans, a yes/no from the customer — or peak-hour operations will kill the program. Measure attachment rate and basket value. If you cannot see which campaigns moved those two numbers, you are running decoration, not cross-sell.
documents.s: What good checkout cross-selling looks like

documents.t: ** In-store retail media means using the screens inside your own stores — especially customer-facing displays at checkout — as a promotion channel, the same way e-commerce sites use their homepages and search results. For physical retailers it is the most under-used media asset they own: every shopper who reaches the counter looks at that screen, at the exact moment a purchase decision is being completed.

Retail media exploded online first: retailers realized their own digital real estate was valuable to brands and to their own promotions. The same logic is now moving into physical stores — and checkout is the natural starting point, because it is the one place in the store where attention is guaranteed. The customer is standing still, facing the counter, waiting for a payment to process. Compare that to the traditional in-store promotion toolkit: Printed posters** — static, slow to change, impossible to localize per store without a print-and-ship cycle. Shelf talkers — seen mid-journey, long before the buying moment. Cashier scripts — inconsistent by nature; every staff member delivers them differently, and busy queues kill them entirely.
documents.s: Why in-store media is having its moment

documents.t: Hanging a TV with a looping video is digital signage. In-store retail media is different in three ways: It reacts to context. The most valuable campaigns respond to what is happening at the register — recommending an add-on that fits what the customer is already buying. It is centrally controlled and locally targeted. One team schedules campaigns by store group, time window, and objective — a rainy-season bundle in Jakarta, a mall-exclusive offer in Orchard — without touching each screen. It is measured. Campaigns tie back to transactions, so you know what a placement did to attachment rate and basket value, not just how many times it played.
documents.s: What separates real in-store media from digital signage

documents.t: You do not need a brand-funded media network on day one. documents.t: ** Inter-store stock transfer optimization is the practice of rebalancing inventory you already own: moving units from stores where they sit idle to stores where they would sell this week. For multi-store retailers it is usually the fastest inventory win available, because it recovers sales and protects margin without spending a single dollar of new purchase budget.

When a store runs short on a selling item, the reflex is to reorder. But a reorder takes supplier lead time, ties up new budget, and often lands after the demand moment has passed. Meanwhile the exact units the store needs are frequently sitting in another store in the same network — already bought, already paid for, quietly aging toward a markdown. Rebalancing that stock does three things at once: Recovers the sale** at the store that had the demand. Rescues the excess at the store that did not, before it needs a discount. Protects purchase budget for genuinely new demand instead of duplicating stock the network already owns.

Broken size runs — a store sells out of core sizes while other stores hold full curves of the same item. Simultaneous shortage and excess — the same SKU is at stockout risk in one location and overstocked in another. Markdown concentration — end-of-season discounts cluster in a few stores, which means allocation (not the product) was the problem. Spreadsheet transfer planning — transfers happen only when a planner has time to build the file, not when the demand signal appears.
documents.s: Signs your network needs transfer optimization

documents.t: Manual transfer planning fails not because planners lack skill but because the decision space is huge: every SKU × size × source store × destination store combination. Optimization tackles it in four steps: Pair excess with shortage. Demand forecasts at store and SKU level identify which locations will run short and which hold more than they can sell. Score by urgency. Not all transfers matter equally — units closest to a lost sale or a markdown move to the top of the queue. Build the route plan. Source, destination, and quantities are laid out on one network view, so logistics cost and effort stay visible. Approve in one click. Planners review a pre-ranked recommendation list and act on dozens of moves in minutes.

documents.t: Omnichannel retail means selling across multiple channels — a physical store, a website, a marketplace, a mobile app — and trying to make the experience consistent between them. In practice, this is often achieved by connecting several separate systems: one for POS, one for e-commerce, one for inventory, stitched together with integrations. Unified commerce goes a step further: instead of separate systems talking to each other, there is one platform underneath every channel. Stock, pricing, promotions and customer profiles live in a single system of record, updated in real time, everywhere. The practical difference shows up the moment something changes. In a loosely-integrated omnichannel setup, a stock update in-store might take minutes (or hours) to reflect online. In a unified commerce platform, it's instant — because there's only one source of truth.

Fashion and lifestyle retail has some specific pressures that make unified commerce especially valuable: Fast-moving stock — collections change seasonally (or faster), so stale inventory data across channels directly costs sales. Buy Online, Pick Up In-Store (BOPIS) and ship-from-store fulfilment only work reliably when every channel sees the same, real-time stock position. Consistent loyalty and customer profiles — a customer's purchase history and loyalty status should look the same whether they're served by a store associate or an online chatbot. Yet many retailers continue to operate with disconnected systems for POS, inventory management, ecommerce, customer loyalty, and store operations. The result is operational inefficiency, inventory inaccuracies, inconsistent customer experiences, and limited visibility across the business. To remain competitive, retailers are increasingly adopting a Unified Commerce Platform—a modern approach that brings every retail operation into a single ecosystem powered by real-time data.

documents.t: Today's consumers expect convenience, speed, and consistency across every touchpoint. A customer may discover a product online, check store availability on their phone, purchase it for store pickup, and later return it through a different channel. Retailers that cannot support these journeys risk losing sales, damaging customer loyalty, and increasing operational costs. The challenge: Most retailers still operate multiple disconnected systems that were never designed for modern omnichannel commerce.
documents.s: The Retail Industry Has Changed Forever

documents.t: Traditional retail environments often rely on separate applications for inventory management, customer relationship management, point of sale, replenishment, reporting, and ecommerce. While these systems may function individually, the lack of integration creates significant business challenges. Business Challenge Impact on Retail Operations Inventory Inaccuracy Lost sales, stockouts, excess inventory Disconnected Customer Data Poor personalization and loyalty engagement Manual Replenishment Slow inventory movement and higher markdowns Limited Reporting Visibility Delayed business decisions Omnichannel Complexity Higher fulfillment costs and customer dissatisfaction
documents.s: The Hidden Cost of Disconnected Retail Systems

documents.t: A Unified Commerce Platform centralizes retail operations into a single architecture where inventory, sales, customer information, store operations, and fulfillment processes share the same data source. Rather than synchronizing multiple systems through complex integrations, every department works from a single version of the truth. This creates real-time visibility across the entire retail organization while simplifying operations and improving customer experiences.
documents.s: What Is a Unified Commerce Platform?

documents.t: Inventory accuracy remains one of the biggest challenges facing retailers. Without real-time inventory visibility, businesses frequently experience stock discrepancies, missed sales opportunities, and unnecessary markdowns. Unified Commerce enables retailers to maintain accurate inventory information across stores, warehouses, and digital channels in real time. Reduce stock discrepancies Improve inventory accuracy Increase product availability Support faster fulfillment decisions

Modern consumers expect flexibility. They want to buy online, pick up in-store, reserve products, transfer items between locations, and return purchases through any channel. Unified Commerce allows retailers to manage these processes through a single workflow rather than multiple disconnected systems. Buy Online Pick Up In Store (BOPIS) Ship From Store Endless Aisle Cross-channel returns Store-to-store fulfillment

Customers expect retailers to recognize them regardless of where they shop. A Unified Commerce Platform consolidates customer interactions, purchase history, loyalty activities, and engagement data into a single customer profile. This enables retailers to deliver more personalized experiences and strengthen customer loyalty.

Traditional replenishment processes often rely on spreadsheets, manual calculations, or outdated sales data. Unified Commerce platforms leverage real-time inventory and sales information to support more intelligent replenishment decisions. Retailers can allocate inventory based on demand, sales performance, stock thresholds, and product life cycle trends.

In today's market, waiting days or weeks for reports is no longer acceptable. Unified Commerce gives decision-makers immediate access to operational data across stores, products, customers, and supply chains. This enables leaders to respond faster to changing consumer behavior and market conditions.

Economic uncertainty, rising operational costs, increasing customer expectations, and growing competition have made retail execution more complex than ever before. Retailers can no longer afford fragmented systems that create inefficiencies and limit visibility. Organizations that embrace Unified Commerce gain significant advantages: Higher inventory accuracy Improved customer satisfaction Reduced operational complexity Faster fulfillment processes Better decision-making capabilities Improved scalability for growth
documents.s: Why Unified Commerce Matters More Than Ever

documents.t: Retail transformation is no longer about adding more technology. It is about connecting every part of the retail operation through a single platform that provides visibility, agility, and control. Unified Commerce empowers retailers to break down operational silos, improve customer experiences, optimize inventory, and support long-term business growth. As customer expectations continue to evolve, retailers that adopt a unified approach will be better positioned to compete, innovate, and scale in an increasingly complex marketplace.

You will be prompted to verify your company/store name and enter your unique User ID and password to establish a connection. documents.t: This error typically occurs if a previous session was not closed correctly, leaving the register "locked" in the system. documents.s: What should I do if I see the error "Register already in use!"?

documents.t: Our Cegid POS support includes a robust Standalone Mode feature. documents.t: Prism supports distributed store activity even during connectivity interruptions. documents.t: Your Point of Sale cannot exist in a vacuum. ERP connectivity and seamless data flow are essential for modern growth. Here's how Retail Pro Prism's advanced architecture supports business expansion.

Prism is built on a modern, web-based architecture using a two-tier direct connection model. A central Point of Authority (POA) or Root Authority (RA) manages enterprise master data — pricing, inventory, promotions — synchronized across any number of distributed store servers. This hierarchical structure keeps the system organized and manageable as you add stores or subsidiaries across regions or countries.
documents.s: What is the fundamental architecture of Retail Pro Prism, and how does it support scalability?

documents.t: Prism is an API-first platform: its core functionality is accessible via a robust REST API. Standard HTTP requests and JSON data structures enable real-time or scheduled data exchange with ERPs, e-commerce webstores and accounting software, keeping your entire technology stack synchronized.
documents.s: How does the Retail Pro Prism API facilitate connectivity with other business systems?

documents.t: Yes. UI customizations use standard web technologies (HTML, CSS, AngularJS). For deeper needs, Event Hooks — such as Tender Events — trigger specific actions, like sending transaction totals to an external loyalty engine or specialized payment terminal, without compromising the core system's integrity.
documents.s: Can we customize the system to meet unique operational requirements?

documents.t: Prism uses an asynchronous, fault-tolerant messaging system (PrismMQ / RabbitMQ). Every business event — a sale, a price change, a new customer profile — is queued and delivered reliably even during temporary network interruptions.
documents.s: How does the system handle high-volume data and ensure reliability during growth?

Modern Windows or Android POS terminal/tablet. Stable internet connection (for cloud-connected features). Compatible barcode scanner, receipt printer and payment terminal.

For on-premise deployments: a dedicated server meeting the vendor's minimum specification for the specific POS platform in use. For cloud deployments: no on-site server required, subject to network requirements (see Network Requirements).

Sales transactions (cash, card, and any other supported payment types). Returns and refunds. Inventory updates after a sale. Reporting and dashboard data accuracy. Network resilience (e.g. behavior during a brief connectivity drop, if applicable). Sign-off from the client is typically obtained before the store goes live.
Administrator — full access, including user and configuration management. Store manager — store-level reporting and operational controls. Cashier/staff — POS transaction access only.
Create individual accounts per staff member rather than sharing logins. Review and remove access promptly when staff leave. Apply the Password Policy.
For deployments that include traffic counting or in-store analytics cameras:

Mount cameras to capture entry/exit points without obstruction. Avoid direct backlighting (e.g. facing large windows or doors) which can reduce detection accuracy. Maintain the manufacturer's recommended mounting height and angle for the specific camera model in use. Confirm camera placement covers 100% of store entrances for accurate footfall counting.
For cloud-hosted deployments:

Provision the client's cloud environment/tenant. Configure connectivity from store locations per Network Requirements. Migrate or load initial data (products, pricing, staff). Configure user accounts and roles. Validate connectivity and performance from each store before go-live.
Importing/exporting product, pricing and customer data. Data cleanup (e.g. merging duplicate customer records). Coordinating data retention per the Data Retention Policy.
Registering new POS terminals, printers and scanners. Monitoring device health/connectivity status. Pushing software updates to devices. Decommissioning and wiping devices no longer in use.

Confirm the Pre-deployment Checklist is complete. Install and configure POS hardware at each till point. Connect hardware to the store network per the Network Requirements. Install and configure the POS/retail software. Load initial product, pricing and staff data. Run through Acceptance Testing before go-live.

Stable internet connection with sufficient bandwidth for POS and reporting traffic. A dedicated VLAN or network segment for POS/retail systems, where possible. Firewall rules allowing outbound access to required cloud endpoints. Redundant connectivity (e.g. backup 4G/5G) recommended for mission-critical, cloud-connected deployments. Specific port/endpoint requirements depend on the solution modules in use — confirm with the technical team.
For on-premise deployments:

Complete Server Installation at the primary site. Deploy POS terminals per the Installation Guide. Configure local network and, if applicable, connectivity back to head office for consolidated reporting. Establish a local backup routine per the Backup Policy.

A typical checklist before starting a deployment: Site survey completed (see Site Survey). Network requirements confirmed (see Network Requirements). Store layout and camera positions planned, if applicable. Hardware (POS terminals, printers, scanners) delivered to site. Staff accounts and roles prepared (see Account/User Management). Go-live date and rollback plan agreed with the client.

Define which KPIs matter for the business (sales, footfall conversion, stock turnover, etc.). Set up dashboards per role (store manager vs head office). Schedule automated report delivery (daily/weekly/monthly) as needed. See also the Reporting solution overview.
For on-premise deployments requiring a local server:

Confirm server hardware meets System Requirements. Install the operating system and required runtime/database components. Install the POS/retail management server software. Configure backups per the Backup Policy. Connect POS terminals to the server over the local network.
For multi-store operators:
Adding and configuring new store locations. Managing per-store settings (pricing, tax, staff assignments). Monitoring store-level performance via Reporting and Dashboard Configuration.
A site survey is typically conducted before installation to confirm the store is ready for deployment.

Physical layout of the store and point-of-sale locations. Existing network infrastructure and Wi-Fi coverage. Power outlet availability at POS and camera locations. Any site-specific constraints (e.g. structural, connectivity). Findings from the site survey feed directly into the Installation Guide and Camera Positioning plan.

POS terminal placement relative to customer flow and queueing. Network cabling / Wi-Fi access point placement for reliable coverage. Camera placement for traffic counting (see Camera Positioning). Space for receipt printers, scanners and payment terminals at each till. Store layout plans are typically reviewed jointly with the client during the Site Survey.

POS terminal offline — check network connectivity first (see Network Requirements). Transaction not syncing — confirm internet connectivity and check for pending sync errors in the admin console. Report data looks wrong — confirm the reporting period/filters, and check for any pending data sync. If the issue persists, contact support with the store name, device ID and a description of the issue.
